opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think geography matters, but maybe not in the way people first assume. There's this idea that if you're not in the Bay Area, you're out of the loop. To some extent that's true: so much of the culture, the gossip, and the density of talent is concentrated there. But in my experience, frontier research ultimately comes down to having a small number of really strong people with a lot of conviction, good taste, and enough compute. None of those are strictly tied to one zip code.

For Singapore specifically, I think there's a lot of untapped talent in this part of the world. Many very strong people grew up here or in the broader region, went abroad to study or work, and would love to come back if there were a place doing genuinely frontier work. For a long time that option didn't really exist. You either moved to the US or you did something that wasn't quite at the cutting edge. So part of the motivation is to create that option and give people a reason to build here.

There are practical advantages too. Singapore is well connected, it's stable, and the government is quite forward-thinking about AI. Being in a different time zone can actually help. You get some distance from the hype cycle of the day and can focus on the work. I'm not going to pretend there are no downsides. You do have to work harder to stay plugged into the global conversation, and recruiting senior people can be harder when they're anchored elsewhere. But research is pretty global now. Papers, models, and ideas move instantly, and you can still be on a call with collaborators anywhere.

So my view is that geography is a factor, not a destiny. If the people are great and the mission is clear, you can do frontier work from Singapore. Honestly, I'd like to help prove that.

r001.rationale: The candidate says geography is a factor, not a destiny, and points out that research, ideas, and collaborators are globally connected, questioning whether a lab must be in one particular location.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I get asked a lot, and honestly my view has evolved over time. When I was at Google Brain, pretty much everything happened in Mountain View, and there's this assumption that frontier AI research has to happen in the Bay Area, because that's where the talent density is, where the compute is, where the capital is, where you bump into people at coffee shops and that's how ideas spread.

And I don't think that's entirely wrong. The density thing is real. But I think people overstate it, especially now. A lot of what actually matters for training a frontier model is not geography, it's compute access, it's having a small team of people who really know what they're doing, and it's just execution. Compute is not in Singapore or in San Francisco, it's in a data center somewhere, and you access it over the network. So from a pure engineering point of view, the physical location of your laptop doesn't matter that much.

Where geography does matter is talent. The question is, can you get the people? And Singapore is interesting because it's small, but it punches above its weight. There's a decent pipeline from NUS and NTU, there's a lot of Southeast Asian talent that wants to stay in the region, and there are people like me who are from here and want to build here. We're not going to get a thousand researchers, but you also don't need a thousand researchers. Some of the best models have been trained by surprisingly small teams.

The other thing is, I actually think being slightly outside the Bay Area echo chamber can be good for you. There's a lot of groupthink in SF. Everyone is working on the same thing at the same time, reading the same tweets. Being a bit removed from that forces you to think from first principles about what you actually want to build rather than what's trending this week.

And then there's the regional angle, which for us is quite important. Southeast Asia is six hundred million-plus people, a lot of languages, a lot of culture that frontier labs in the US just don't prioritize because it's not their market. Being here means we actually care about that, and we have the context to do it well. So I'd say geography is less of a constraint than people think, and in some ways it's a feature.

r001.rationale: The candidate argues that geography matters less because compute is accessed over a network and a researcher’s laptop location matters little. It does not mention researchers collaborating across geographically distributed teams.

astra-6.text:
I think geography matters a lot for building a team, but it shouldn’t define the ambition of the lab. If you’re building a frontier AI lab in Singapore, the goal has to be to do research that’s competitive globally. Being the best lab in Singapore isn’t enough.

The practical question is talent: who can you bring together, and who would want to build their life there? Some people want to be in the Bay Area, but there are also great researchers who want to stay in Asia or come back to Asia. A lab in Singapore gives those people another place to do ambitious work.

At the same time, you can’t assume that location alone gives you an advantage. You still need compute, a strong research culture, and people who can execute. So I’d think of Singapore as the place where you build the team, while keeping the research agenda and the standard you hold yourself to global.

r001.rationale: The response says geography matters for team building and discusses talent preferences, but it does not question location’s importance on the basis that researchers already collaborate across distributed teams.

sol-6.1.text:
I think geography matters, but it’s not destiny. If you’re building a frontier lab in Singapore, the question is: can you bring together the right people, give them enough compute, and create an environment where they can do really ambitious research?

There are advantages to being in the Bay Area. The density of researchers, founders, and capital makes a lot of things easier. You shouldn’t underestimate that. But I also don’t think all the people capable of doing frontier research happen to live in one place. There’s talent in Singapore and across Asia, including people who would prefer to build their careers here.

The important thing is that being based in Singapore shouldn’t mean setting a smaller ambition. You want to contribute to the global frontier, stay connected to the international research community, and build a place that great researchers want to join. Location can help shape that institution, but ultimately the work has to speak for itself.

r001.rationale: The response says geography matters and notes that talent exists across locations, but it does not question geography’s importance on the grounds that researchers already collaborate across distributed teams.
